content: Orthodontic treatment sometimes requires moving the upper first molars backward (distalising) to create space or manage anchorage needs. This can be achieved using either extraoral or intraoral appliances. Extraoral headgear is a common method, but it demands significant patient cooperation and has been associated with reports of serious injuries. To address these limitations, intraoral appliances have been developed. However, the comparative effectiveness of extraoral and intraoral appliances has not been thoroughly evaluated. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of orthodontic treatment aimed at distalising upper first molars in children and adolescents. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Group's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to December 10, 2012. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date during the search. The review included randomized clinical trials that investigated the use of removable or fixed orthodontic appliances for distalising upper first molars in children and adolescents. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were followed, including independent data extraction and risk of bias assessment. Authors of the studies were contacted to clarify inclusion criteria. Ten studies involving 354 participants were included in the review. Most studies were conducted in university dental hospital settings in Europe and Brazil, with publication dates ranging from 2005 to 2011. Participants were aged between 9 and 15 years, with an even gender distribution in seven studies and a slight predominance of females in three studies. The overall quality of the studies was poor, with seven studies at high risk of bias, three at unclear risk, and none at low risk of bias. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed for primary clinical outcomes, such as the movement of upper first molars (measured in millimeters) and loss of anterior anchorage, when sufficient data were available. Four studies, involving 159 participants, compared a distalising appliance to an untreated control group. However, meta-analyses could not be conducted for all primary outcomes due to incomplete reporting of summary statistics, expected outcomes, and differences in appliance types. The degree and direction of molar movement and anterior anchorage loss varied depending on the type of appliance used. Four studies, involving 150 participants, compared intraoral distalising appliances to headgear. The mean molar movement achieved with intraoral appliances was -2.20 mm, compared to -1.04 mm with headgear. This difference was statistically significant, favoring intraoral appliances (mean difference: -1.45 mm; 95% confidence interval: -2.74 to -0.15). However, headgear was associated with less loss of anterior anchorage, as indicated by statistically significant differences in mean mesial upper incisor movement (1.82 mm; 95% CI: 1.39 to 2.24) and overjet (1.64 mm; 95% CI: 1.26 to 2.02). These findings suggest that while intraoral appliances are more effective at distalising molars, they result in greater loss of anterior anchorage compared to headgear. Direct comparisons of different intraoral appliances were reported narratively due to variations in interventions across studies. All appliances were found to provide some degree of distal molar movement, but the extent of anterior anchorage loss varied depending on the appliance type. None of the included studies reported on adverse effects, such as harm or injury, nor did they provide data on the number of patient visits or rates of non-compliance. In conclusion, intraoral appliances appear to be more effective than headgear for distalising upper first molars. However, this advantage is offset by a greater loss of anterior anchorage, which was not observed with headgear in the limited number of studies available. The evidence base for orthodontic treatment aimed at distalising upper first molars is small and of low or very low quality.
